newsitem.title: UK: Dollar retreats in late Europe but focus on upside.
newsitem.headline: Dollar retreats in late Europe but focus on upside.

text.p: The dollar took a step back in late Europe after earlier powering to its strongest levels in years, but sentiment remained resolutely upbeat.
Though the session lacked major U.S. data or news, a bullish tide swept the dollar to 1.6001 marks -- its best level since July 1994 -- before profit takers lobbed it back below 1.59.

"I wouldn't be surprised if we have a bit of a correction, but overall I don't think there's any major change in the attitude towards the dollar," said Peter Wood, forex dealer at Bank of Boston in London. The 1.60 level was an objective for many, so selling there was no cause for concern, he added.
The dollar was quoted at 1.5866/76 marks by 1610 GMT, its softest level of the European session and down from 1.5960/65 here late on Tuesday.
Dollar/yen soared to a 46-month peak of 117.48 intrasession before slipping to 116.93/7.03 in late trade, not far off 116.91/96 late yesterday.

Traders said concern over the health of Russian president Boris Yeltsin had provoked some selling. The chief Kremlin doctor said today that Yeltsin had a "fairly serious illness" and should stay in hospital until the end of the week because of the risk of complications in his pneumonia.
Peter von Maydell, senior currency economist at UBS, said currency markets were getting ahead of bond markets.

"The bond markets still support the dollar in terms of the yield differential but they're not making any new highs in terms of spreads, so I think the dollar's going to have to consolidate for a while," he said.
Dollar/mark was set to travel above 1.60 again eventually, while dollar/yen should also hit new highs, he said.
Analysts pointed to today's Japanese newspaper report quoting a Bank of Japan official as saying that the central bank will maintain its low interest rate policy for the time being.
Problems in the financial sector, falling land prices and overextended property prices were also yen-negative, they said.
"Everything's in place for more (yen) depreciation, and I think that's going to be a feature for a long, long time to come," said Von Maydell.
The dollar was quoted at 1.3730/40 Swiss francs at 1639 GMT, off its earlier 31-month peak of 1.3808 and down from Tuesday's closing European level of 1.3778/87.
Elsewhere, UK markets were on rate-hike watch as Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke held his regular monetary meeting with Bank of England governor Eddie George.
Previously widespread market expectations of an increase in the 6.0 percent base rate have been considerably weakened in recent days by a string of soft UK economic data.

Because the monetary meeting began after the Bank of England had ended its daily money market operations, any decision on rates is unlikely to be known until tomorrow's first round of money market operations, between 0950 and 1000 GMT.
Sterling stood at $1.6770/75 and 2.6672/82 marks at 1650 GMT compared with yesterday's late European rates of $1.6680/85 and 2.6610/20.
